To traduce someone means to deliberately say false and damaging things about them to other people, in order to destroy or harm their reputation.

Think of it as a combination of lying about someone and spreading those lies — both elements must be present. The goal, whether stated or implied, is to make that person look bad in the eyes of others.

Imagine your colleague did excellent work on a project. But your boss, out of jealousy, goes around telling everyone that your colleague cheated, plagiarized, and took credit for others' ideas — none of which is true.

Your boss has traduced your colleague.

Three things happened:

  • The statements were false
  • They were spread to other people
  • They were designed to damage how others see that person

All three of those things together = traducing someone.
What Makes It Different From Just "Lying" or "Criticizing"

This is important. Traduce is a very specific kind of wrongdoing, not just any negative talk.

  • If you criticize someone using true facts, that is not traducing them.
  • If you lie to someone about yourself, that is not traducing anyone.
  • If you privately hold a false, bad opinion of someone but say nothing, that is not traducing.

Traducing requires falseness + spreading + targeting a specific person's reputation. All three together.
How It Feels in a Sentence

The word carries a strong sense of moral wrongness — an injustice done to an innocent person. Read these:

  • "The politician was traduced by his opponents, who spread lies about his past to the media."
  • "She felt helpless as her former friend traduced her name across the entire school."
  • "History has sometimes traduced great thinkers, branding them as dangerous when they were merely ahead of their time."

Notice the feeling each sentence carries: a victim who didn't deserve what happened to them, and someone doing something genuinely cruel and dishonest.
The Register: When Is This Word Used?

Traduce is a formal, literary word. You won't typically hear it in casual everyday conversation. You're far more likely to encounter it in:

  • Serious journalism or political writing
  • Literature and fiction
  • Formal speeches or essays
  • Legal or academic discussions about defamation

In everyday speech, people would instead say someone was slandered, badmouthed, smeared, lied about, or defamed. Traduce carries all of these meanings but in a more elevated, weighty way. Choosing the word "traduce" signals that the act being described is considered a serious moral offence, not just casual gossip.
Similar Words — And How Traduce Sits Among Them

Understanding a word fully means knowing its neighbors.

Slander means making false spoken statements about someone. Traduce overlaps with this almost entirely, but traduce emphasizes the deliberate, targeted nature of the act more strongly.

Defame is the broadest term — it simply means damaging someone's reputation, whether through lies or even technically true but misleading statements. Traduce is narrower: it specifically involves false statements.

Malign means to speak badly of someone, but the statements don't have to be false. You can malign someone with the truth. You cannot traduce them with the truth.

Vilify means to attack someone verbally in a very harsh, extreme way, making them seem evil. Traduce focuses more on misrepresentation, while vilify focuses more on the severity and cruelty of the attack.

Calumniate is the closest synonym to traduce — almost identical in meaning. Both mean making false and harmful statements about someone. Calumniate is perhaps even rarer and more archaic. If you know "traduce," you essentially know "calumniate" too.

Traduce can also extend slightly beyond spoken or written lies. It can refer to misrepresenting someone's ideas, beliefs, or character in a way that distorts who they really are — even if no single sentence is an outright lie. For example:

"The documentary traduced the scientist by selectively editing her words to make her sound like a fraud."

Here, individual clips might be technically real, but the overall picture presented is false and damaging. This broader sense — to distort and misrepresent in a way that harms — is a valid and common use of traduce.
The One-Line Summary to Remember Forever

To traduce someone = to lie about them to others in order to damage what people think of them.

If you remember that single sentence and the examples above, you have this word completely mastered.
